answer.question: Does Broomfield's landscape code let me put artificial turf in my backyard?
answer.answer: Likely, but get it in writing. The revised code names single-unit backyards among the places turf can go, yet the city's own page says the new rules don't affect single-unit landscaping at all. Ask Planning and Development Services which applies.

blocks.h2: Broomfield names artificial turf and tells you where it can go.
blocks.takeaway: The code names artificial turf for single-unit backyards, athletic fields and purpose-built dog parks — not a strip by the street. We measure that boundary at the free visit before drawing your layout.
paras: Ordinance No. 2291, adopted by Broomfield's city council on 13 January 2026, revised Chapter 17-70 of the Broomfield Municipal Code and named artificial turf directly. Under the update, artificial turf is named in three places: athletic fields of play, the backyards of single-unit residential lots, and dog parks built specifically for that use.

That's the list the ordinance names, and a strip beside the street or a shared common area isn't on it. Whether it also covers a single-unit home's front yard is a real question — Broomfield's own page cuts against itself on that point, and the next section walks you through it. Plan your project around the backyard the code clearly names, and treat anything visible from the street as the edge of what's settled for now. On the free visit we measure that boundary, along with the slope and drainage across it, before we draw a layout, so the footprint we propose matches the yard the code allows, not just the yard you'd like to fill.

blocks.kicker: Read this before you assume it applies to you
blocks.h2: The city says the new code doesn't touch a single-unit home's yard at all.
blocks.takeaway: The city's own page contradicts itself on whether the code reaches your backyard at all. Ask Broomfield Planning and Development Services for a written answer before you commit to a footprint.
paras: The same Broomfield Voice page that lists where turf can go also says something that cuts the other way: "The new regulations do not impact landscaping for single-unit residential properties, including both attached and detached homes." Read one way, that's reassurance — a single-family backyard project sits outside the ordinance's technical standards entirely. Read the other way, it sits inside the permitted-use list from the same document. Both can't be the operating rule for your address.

Don't guess which reading applies. Ask Broomfield's Planning and Development Services whether Chapter 17-70's technical standards govern a backyard turf conversion at a detached or attached single-unit home, and get the answer in writing before you commit to a footprint. Colorado's own turf law works on a similar split — it reaches HOA common areas, commercial sites and larger multifamily buildings, and leaves a single-family backyard alone. Our Colorado turf law guide covers what the state controls, so you know which questions are Broomfield's to answer and which are the state's.

blocks.h2: Three days a week, and turf needs none of them.
blocks.takeaway: Broomfield caps watering at three days a week, drought or not, on days set by your address. A converted backyard has no schedule to track, because it never needs watering.
paras: Broomfield's Water Use Ordinance took effect on 1 January 2025 and runs whether or not a drought is declared. Watering is limited to no more than three days a week, only between 6 p.m. and 10 a.m., on a schedule set by your address: even-numbered addresses water Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and odd-numbered addresses water Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday. A leaking sprinkler head has to be fixed within ten days, and hosing down a driveway or patio with water isn't allowed except for a public health or safety reason.

None of that schedule touches a converted backyard once the turf is down. There's no address parity to track, no ten-day repair clock on a system that isn't there, and nothing to check before deciding whether today is a watering day — because it never is one.

blocks.h2: A voluntary ask on top of the ordinance, and it can change fast.
blocks.takeaway: Since February 2026, a voluntary Drought Watch asks for two watering days a week, and it can change without much notice. Check the current stage before planning anything else that still needs water.
paras: Broomfield declared a Drought Watch on 9 February 2026. It's voluntary: the city asks residents to limit watering to no more than two days a week, tighter than the Water Use Ordinance's three-day cap but not enforced the way that ordinance is. As of today, mandatory restrictions aren't in place.

A Drought Watch is also the kind of thing that can change without much notice, as snowpack and deliveries shift through the season. Ask us on the free visit, or check the city's page, for the current stage before you finish planning anything else in the yard that still needs water. A backyard already converted to turf doesn't need to track any of it.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Broomfield, CO?
faq.a: We install artificial turf, backyard putting greens and pet turf in Broomfield, CO. The city's landscape code, revised by Ordinance No. 2291, permits artificial turf in the backyards of single-unit residential lots, and its Water Use Ordinance limits watering to three days a week whether or not a drought is declared — turf needs none of those days. Call 303-349-2368 to set up a free visit.

faq.q: Where in my yard does Broomfield's code let me put artificial turf?
faq.a: The backyard, if you're on a single-unit lot. Ordinance No. 2291 names artificial turf in athletic fields of play, single-unit backyards, and purpose-built dog parks (City of Broomfield). A strip beside the street isn't on that list. A front yard is a separate, open question — see the next question below.

faq.q: Does the new landscape code even apply to my single-family home?
faq.a: The city's own page reads both ways. It lists single-unit backyards among the places turf is permitted, and in the same breath says the new regulations "do not impact landscaping for single-unit residential properties, including both attached and detached homes" (City of Broomfield). Ask Broomfield Planning and Development Services which reading applies to your address, and get the answer in writing before you plan a footprint.

faq.q: How many days a week can I water in Broomfield right now?
faq.a: Up to three, under the Water Use Ordinance in effect since 1 January 2025 — even-numbered addresses on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, odd-numbered on Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday, only between 6 p.m. and 10 a.m. (City of Broomfield). A voluntary Drought Watch declared 9 February 2026 asks residents to cut that to two days (City of Broomfield). Turf doesn't need any of those days.

faq.q: Is artificial turf illegal in Colorado?
faq.a: No — Colorado hasn't banned it. State law reaches nonfunctional turf on HOA common areas, commercial sites and larger multifamily buildings, and leaves a single-family backyard alone. Our Colorado turf law guide covers what the state controls and what's left to Broomfield's own code.
